query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In pre‐exposure Q235 steel, the degree of corrosion degradation versus protection in both room‐temperature and high‐temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt environments is controlled by the stability and adherence of the native iron-oxide scale. In particular, if the protective oxide (e.g. a magnetite/spinel layer) formed under these conditions can withstand thermally induced phase transformations and spallation, then it buffers the corrosive attack; however, if high temperatures trigger transformation (e.g. to a less-protective hematite form) or cause detachment of the oxide scale, then accelerated corrosion (mass gain/loss) will occur.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with its naturally formed thin native oxide film.
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel specimens to an aggressive salt environment at two controlled temperature regimes – one at room temperature and another at high temperatures (700–900 °C) – in an otherwise identical, controlled atmosphere.
generation.conditions: All samples are immersed in the same aggressive molten salt medium (with defined composition as used in high-temperature corrosion studies) for a fixed duration. Environmental parameters such as salt composition, exposure time, and ambient pressure are held constant; only temperature is varied between room temperature and high-temperature regimes. Evaluation is via mass change measurements and detailed oxide scale characterization (using techniques like SEM, EDS, and XRD) after exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, phase, and adhesion of the oxide scale (i.e., whether it remains as a protective magnetite/spinel or transforms/spalls into a non-protective oxide such as hematite) at the steel–environment interface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the native oxide (primarily magnetite or a mixed iron oxide) remains adherent and protective. At 700–900 °C in the salt, thermal energy can promote phase transitions or differential thermal expansion that may destabilize the oxide scale – either causing it to convert to a less-protective phase (e.g. hematite) or to spall off from the surface. This loss or transformation exposes the iron substrate to accelerated corrosive attack, leading to notable mass change and microstructural degradation. Thus, the integrity of the oxide barrier dictates whether corrosion protection persists or fails.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the room-temperature reference, Q235 steel exposed to high-temperature salt will exhibit a significantly different mass change (either greater mass loss due to substrate attack or anomalous gain due to poorly adherent corrosion products) and clear evidence of oxide phase transformation or spallation. If the protective oxide remains stable at high temperature, minimal additional degradation would be observed; however, if destabilized, the corrosion rate will be markedly higher.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples exposed to the same salt environment at room temperature, where the native oxide remains intact and ensures limited corrosion, serve as the reference condition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under oxidizing salt conditions that permit the formation (and possible transformation) of a native iron oxide scale. It may not hold in environments that do not support significant oxide formation or when mechanical stresses (other than thermal cycling) dominate the failure mode.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall role of oxide scale stability in high-temperature corrosion is well recognized from similar studies, the exact phase composition, transformation temperature, and adhesion behavior of the native oxide on Q235 steel in the specific salt mixture remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Q235 steel samples in the pre-exposure state and subject them to identical aggressive salt immersion tests at room temperature and at 700–900 °C for a set duration. After exposure, perform mass change measurements and detailed oxide scale analysis (via SEM/EDS and XRD) to identify oxide phases and assess adherence. Additionally, control samples pre-treated to deliberately remove any oxide layer should be tested to confirm the role of the oxide.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after high-temperature salt exposure, the protective oxide scale on Q235 steel remains phase-pure, adherent, and unchanged relative to room temperature conditions (i.e. no significant phase transformation or spallation is observed) and the mass change does not significantly differ from the room-temperature baseline, then the hypothesis that oxide scale destabilization governs the transition from protection to degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Mass change per unit area of the FCC HEA was compared to that of 316 H stainless steel as a reference material tested under identical conditions, and the results are shown in Fig. 4. The results show that the HEA experienced a significantly higher mass loss due to elemental dissolution in the FLiBe salt, of about 3.4 mg/cm2, compared to 0.26 mg/cm2 mass loss in the reference 316 H stainless steel. This large difference in mass loss indicates that elemental dissolution occurred more rapidly in the HEA than 316 H stainless steel. To evaluate the depth of attack, EDS line scans on the sample cross-section were performed. Edge to edge scan showed that all elements maintain the nominal alloy composition throughout the thickness of the sample, except for Mn which shows a depletion in the near-surface regions at both edges as shown in Fig. 5A. Figure 5B shows a higher resolution scan close to the sample surface. The line scan confirms Mn depletion that extends to over 100 µm from the surface and shows discrete spots with noticeably higher Cr concentration.
